title: Six Writing criteria
canonical_rule: OET Writing is assessed on Purpose, Content, Conciseness & Clarity, Genre & Style, Organisation & Layout, and Language. Purpose is scored 0-3; the other five criteria are scored 0-7.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Make purpose immediately apparent
canonical_rule: The reader should understand at the beginning why the letter is being written and why it requires attention.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Personalise the purpose
canonical_rule: State the reason for writing in a way that is specific to this patient and this request rather than relying on a generic memorised opener.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Expand the purpose later
canonical_rule: After the initial high-level purpose, provide the relevant details needed for the reader to act appropriately.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Use the writing task first
canonical_rule: In most tasks, the Writing task states the purpose. If it is incomplete, use the final case-note section immediately above it to clarify the required action/context.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Choose verbs that match the task
canonical_rule: Do not use refer automatically. Depending on the task, verbs such as transfer, see, discharge, accept, update, request, recommend or provide may better express purpose.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Include what the reader needs
canonical_rule: Select information that enables the specific reader to understand the situation, continue care and complete the request.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Exclude what the reader does not need
canonical_rule: Not every case note belongs in the letter; omit details that do not affect the reader’s role in the patient’s care.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Reader relationship changes relevance
canonical_rule: Consider whether the reader already knows the patient and what information will be new or useful to that reader.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Reader role changes relevance
canonical_rule: Select content according to the aspect of care the reader will manage, not according to a fixed list of always-include facts.
evidence: OET Ultimate Writing Guide (official)
ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Represent case notes accurately
canonical_rule: Paraphrase and summarise without changing factual meaning, timing, certainty, medication details, living arrangements, laterality or other clinically material information.

ai_grading_logic: Apply this rule in context; judge effect on OET criterion, clarity, accuracy, and professional communication rather than matching a fixed template.

title: Do not replace patient wording with a stronger diagnosis
canonical_rule: Paraphrase only when meaning and certainty remain identical.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment

bad_example: She has fatigue.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Non-compliance language requires care

title: Unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably are banned as emotional wording
canonical_rule: Emotive/editorialising adverbs (unfortunately, fortunately, regrettably) and dramatised suffering/suffered must not appear in OET Writing Model Answers; state clinical facts and outcomes factually and objectively. Standard clinical usage of suffering/suffered for a diagnosed event (e.g. "suffered a myocardial infarction") is not emotional wording and remains acceptable.
evidence: Writing Rule Enforcement Addendum Rev5 (10 Sep 2026) owner governance decision, item 1 "G-W-116": the newer clarification supersedes this rule's prior general-English framing per the addendum's own precedence rule.
good_example: The scan could not be completed because of severe claustrophobia.
bad_example: Unfortunately, the poor patient could not tolerate the scan.
ai_grading_logic: Flag any use of unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably, and flag suffering/suffered only when paired with a dramatising intensifier (e.g. "suffered terribly", "the poor patient suffered"). Do not flag suffering/suffered used as the standard factual clinical verb for a diagnosed event.
notes: Superseded the original "do not auto-penalise the word itself" framing on 10 Sep 2026 per explicit owner governance decision; see docs/canonical-rules/README.md change log.

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: It started three - sorry, four - days ago.
bad_example: The AI penalises any self-correction automatically.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Pauses can be communicative

evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: I’m sorry to hear that. [brief pause] What is worrying you most right now?
bad_example: Continuous rapid speech with no room for the patient.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Full stops end complete sentences
canonical_rule: Use a full stop to separate complete statements where no stronger relation needs punctuation.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The wound was red. A swab was taken.
bad_example: The wound was red A swab was taken.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Comma after introductory subordinate clause
canonical_rule: A comma usually follows an initial subordinate clause before the main clause.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: When she returned, the swelling had reduced.
bad_example: When she returned the swelling had reduced.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Comma with nonessential appositives
canonical_rule: Use paired commas around nonessential appositive information.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Ms Ali, a 54-year-old teacher, presented with dizziness.
bad_example: Ms Ali, a 54-year-old teacher presented with dizziness.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: No comma between subject and verb
canonical_rule: Do not separate a subject from its verb unless a parenthetical element requires paired commas.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The results of the blood tests were normal.
bad_example: The results of the blood tests, were normal.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Comma before coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
canonical_rule: A comma is commonly used before and/but/so when each side is an independent clause; it may be omitted when clauses are short and closely linked, depending on style.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She remained febrile, so blood cultures were obtained.
bad_example: She remained febrile so, blood cultures were obtained.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Semicolon links closely related independent clauses
canonical_rule: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The pain improved; mobility remained limited.
bad_example: The pain improved; and mobility remained limited.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: A semicolon before a coordinating conjunction is usually unnecessary.

title: Colon introduces an explanation/list after a complete lead-in
canonical_rule: Use a colon after an independent clause that introduces a list, explanation, or elaboration.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She has two current concerns: pain and poor sleep.
bad_example: Her concerns are: pain and poor sleep.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: The second is common but many style guides avoid a colon directly after a linking verb.

title: Apostrophe for possession
canonical_rule: Use ’s for most singular nouns/names; for plural nouns ending in s, add an apostrophe. Style guides vary for singular names ending in s, so be consistent.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Mr Jones’s medication / Mr Jones’ medication (style-dependent)
bad_example: Mr Jones medication
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Do not use apostrophes for ordinary plurals
canonical_rule: Plural nouns and abbreviations normally do not take an apostrophe merely to form the plural.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: GPs; MRIs; 1990s
bad_example: GP’s; MRI’s; 1990’s
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Hyphenate compound modifiers before nouns
canonical_rule: Hyphenate multiword modifiers when needed to prevent ambiguity.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: a six-week history; a 25-year-old patient
bad_example: a six weeks history; a 25 years old patient
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: No hyphen when age/duration is predicative
canonical_rule: Do not use the compound-modifier form after the verb.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She is 25 years old.
bad_example: She is 25-year-old.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Capitalise sentence starts and proper nouns
canonical_rule: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and proper names, institutions, branded medicines, and eponyms as appropriate.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Parkinson disease; City Hospital; Panadol
bad_example: parkinson disease; city hospital; panadol
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Style varies between Parkinson disease and Parkinson’s disease; both are used professionally.

title: Common disease names are normally lowercase
canonical_rule: Generic disease/condition names are lowercase unless they contain a proper noun or begin a sentence.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: hypertension; asthma; myocardial infarction
bad_example: Hypertension; Asthma; Myocardial Infarction
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Generic drug names lowercase; brand names capitalised
canonical_rule: Use lowercase for generic names and the manufacturer’s capitalization for brands.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: paracetamol; amoxicillin; Panadol
bad_example: Paracetamol; Amoxicillin; panadol
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: At sentence start, a generic name is capitalised normally.

title: Use abbreviations only when appropriate to the reader
canonical_rule: Spell out unfamiliar or ambiguous abbreviations; widely understood healthcare abbreviations may be acceptable when the reader’s expertise supports them.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on first mention, then MRI
bad_example: An unexplained local abbreviation.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Avoid note-form dosing abbreviations in a formal letter when clarity may suffer
canonical_rule: Translate ambiguous Latin/frequency abbreviations into plain professional English unless the task/recipient convention clearly supports them.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily
bad_example: amoxicillin 500 mg tds
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: The AI should not mark a recognised abbreviation wrong solely because it is abbreviated; assess audience and clarity.

title: Use numerals with measurements
canonical_rule: Use numerals with doses, measurements, vital signs, ages when paired with units, dates, and exact clinical values.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
bad_example: five hundred mg; thirty-eight point five °C
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Use a space between number and most SI units
canonical_rule: In standard scientific style, place a space between a number and unit symbol, except conventional exceptions such as % depending on house style.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: 500 mg; 5 cm
bad_example: 500mg; 5cm
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: OET does not grade typography as a scientific journal; do not over-penalise accepted variants if clear.

title: Keep decimal points and dose units exact
canonical_rule: Do not alter decimal places, units, or magnitude when paraphrasing case notes.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: 0.5 mg
bad_example: 5 mg
ai_grading_logic: Treat a dose/unit change as a high-severity accuracy error, not merely a grammar error.

title: Do not invent reference ranges
canonical_rule: Report clinically relevant values from the case notes; do not add normal ranges or interpretations not supplied unless the task explicitly provides/requests them.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Her potassium was 3.1 mmol/L.
bad_example: Her potassium was 3.1 mmol/L (normal 3.5–5.0) when the range was not in the notes.
ai_grading_logic: Penalise invented clinical data as Content/accuracy, regardless of grammatical correctness.

title: Word-vs-numeral style is secondary to clarity and consistency
canonical_rule: There is no universal OET rule that 1–9 must always be words and 10+ numerals. Use a consistent professional style; numerals are preferred for clinical data.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She has two children and takes 5 mg daily.
bad_example: She has 2 children and takes five mg daily.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Both child-count styles can be acceptable; the dose should remain numerical.

title: Prefer precise clinical-neutral wording
canonical_rule: Choose words that accurately represent the notes without adding judgement or emotional colouring.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: He reported smoking 20 cigarettes daily.
bad_example: He is a terrible heavy smoker.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Patient is not a forbidden word
canonical_rule: “Patient” is acceptable when natural and unambiguous; avoid repetitive or dehumanising use, not the word itself.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The patient was discharged with community follow-up.
bad_example: Never use the word patient.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: This explicitly overrides the legacy blanket prohibition.

title: Smoker/drinker are not grammatically forbidden but person-first factual wording is often better
canonical_rule: Use factual behaviour descriptions when they are clearer and less judgmental.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She smokes 10 cigarettes per day.
bad_example: She is a smoker.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: “Smoker” is standard English and not automatically an OET error; judge tone/context.

title: Do not replace patient wording with a stronger diagnosis
canonical_rule: Paraphrase only when meaning and certainty remain identical.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She reported feeling tired.
bad_example: She has fatigue.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: “Fatigue” may be a clinical symptom, but it is not always semantically identical to ordinary tiredness.

title: Non-compliance language requires care
canonical_rule: Prefer descriptive, non-judgmental language such as difficulty adhering when supported; “non-compliant” may be accepted if it is the exact case-note concept but can sound judgmental.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: He reported difficulty taking the tablets consistently.
bad_example: He is a non-compliant patient.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably are banned as emotional wording
canonical_rule: Emotive/editorialising adverbs (unfortunately, fortunately, regrettably) and dramatised suffering/suffered must not appear in OET Writing Model Answers; state clinical facts and outcomes factually and objectively. Standard clinical usage of suffering/suffered for a diagnosed event (e.g. "suffered a myocardial infarction") is not emotional wording and remains acceptable.
evidence: Writing Rule Enforcement Addendum Rev5 (10 Sep 2026) owner governance decision, item 1 "G-W-116": the newer clarification supersedes this rule's prior general-English framing per the addendum's own precedence rule.
good_example: The scan could not be completed because of severe claustrophobia.
bad_example: Unfortunately, the poor patient could not tolerate the scan.
ai_grading_logic: Flag any use of unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably, and flag suffering/suffered only when paired with a dramatising intensifier (e.g. "suffered terribly", "the poor patient suffered"). Do not flag suffering/suffered used as the standard factual clinical verb for a diagnosed event.
notes: Superseded the original "do not auto-penalise the word itself" framing on 10 Sep 2026 per explicit owner governance decision; see docs/canonical-rules/README.md change log.

title: Use formal contractions sparingly or not at all in letters
canonical_rule: Full forms are normally preferred in formal healthcare correspondence.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She did not attend.
bad_example: She didn’t attend.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: A contraction is a genre/style issue, not a catastrophic grammar failure.

title: Avoid vague nouns and verbs when precise data are available
canonical_rule: Replace vague “thing/problem/stuff/get” wording with accurate clinical or functional language.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She developed a pruritic rash after the first dose.
bad_example: She got a bad thing after the medicine.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Use person-centred respectful language
canonical_rule: Avoid language that stereotypes, blames, belittles, or reduces a person to a condition.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: A person with diabetes / Ms Chen has diabetes.
bad_example: a diabetic woman
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Some shorthand remains common clinically; OET Genre & Style rewards respectful, reader-appropriate language.

title: Do not invent clinical synonyms
canonical_rule: A “synonym” must preserve the exact meaning, severity, site, timing, and certainty.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: reduced appetite -> decreased appetite
bad_example: haemoptysis -> coughing a lot
ai_grading_logic: Treat meaning-changing paraphrase as Content accuracy, not merely vocabulary style.

title: One paragraph should have a clear information function
canonical_rule: Group related facts by purpose, chronology, clinical issue, or care task; avoid mixing unrelated history and plan in one sentence chain.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Paragraph 1: current problem; Paragraph 2: relevant history/management; final paragraph: request/plan.
bad_example: Random case-note order.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Chronology must be recoverable
canonical_rule: Use tense, time expressions, and paragraph order so the reader can reconstruct what happened and what is current.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Initially..., two days later..., on today’s review...
bad_example: Later... previously... today... last month... in a confusing sequence.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Use time markers only when they add meaning
canonical_rule: Exact dates are useful when clinically important; elapsed time or sequence markers may be clearer otherwise.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Two weeks later, her symptoms worsened.
bad_example: On 03/02/2026, on 05/02/2026, on 07/02/2026... for every minor event.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Avoid repeating the purpose verbatim
canonical_rule: State the purpose early, then expand the actionable details later without mechanically copying the same sentence.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: I am referring... [later] Please assess her recurrent syncope and advise on management.
bad_example: I am referring... I am referring... I am referring...
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Use comparative forms correctly
canonical_rule: Use -er/more and than for comparisons; do not double-mark comparison.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Her pain is worse than yesterday.
bad_example: Her pain is more worse than yesterday.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Use adverbs to modify verbs/adjectives appropriately
canonical_rule: Choose adjective vs adverb according to grammatical function.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The wound healed well. / The wound is well healed.
bad_example: The wound healed good.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Coordinate adjectives can take commas
canonical_rule: Use a comma between coordinate adjectives that independently modify the same noun; do not automatically comma all adjective sequences.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: a severe, persistent headache
bad_example: a small, red blood cell count
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: The second phrase is semantically odd; adjective order and meaning matter.

title: Enough/too patterns
canonical_rule: Use adjective + enough; too + adjective; enough + noun.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She is well enough to return home. / The pain is too severe for discharge.
bad_example: She is enough well to return home.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: That-clauses are valid after report/state/mention
canonical_rule: Reported that + finite clause is standard and not prohibited; gerund/noun alternatives may be more concise.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She reported that the pain had worsened. / She reported worsening pain.
bad_example: She reported that the pain worsened yesterday is always wrong.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Backshift depends on time reference and meaning; do not force one template.

title: Do not backshift current facts unnecessarily
canonical_rule: If information remains true/current, present tense may remain in a that-clause.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She stated that she is allergic to penicillin.
bad_example: She stated that she was allergic to penicillin.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Both may be acceptable; the present tense emphasises that the allergy remains current.

title: Medication lists require unambiguous pairing
canonical_rule: When listing multiple medicines, ensure each name remains paired with the correct dose/frequency/route; punctuation is flexible if meaning is clear.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: metformin 500 mg twice daily; atorvastatin 20 mg nightly
bad_example: metformin 500 mg, atorvastatin twice daily 20 mg
ai_grading_logic: Prioritise correct pairing over a prescribed semicolon template.

title: Laterality and anatomy must remain attached to the finding
canonical_rule: Keep left/right, upper/lower, tooth number, level, and anatomical site with the correct symptom/finding.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: a 6 mm left ureteric calculus
bad_example: a 6 mm ureteric calculus on the right
ai_grading_logic: A laterality change is a high-severity content error.

title: Use ranges and frequencies unambiguously
canonical_rule: Write frequencies so a reader cannot confuse interval, count, or duration.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: every 8 hours; three times daily; for 7 days
bad_example: 8/24; 3/7 when the notation could be ambiguous
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Legacy fraction shorthand must not be automatically decoded unless the source convention is certain.

title: Do not infer shorthand beyond evidence
canonical_rule: If a case-note abbreviation/fraction is ambiguous, preserve only what can be safely interpreted or flag for human review.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Review in three weeks (when the notes clearly mean 3/52).
bad_example: Automatically convert 3/52 to three times a year.
ai_grading_logic: The AI should never hallucinate a dosing/scheduling interpretation from ambiguous shorthand.

title: Meaning-changing language errors are high severity
canonical_rule: Grammar/vocabulary errors that alter medication, dose, laterality, diagnosis certainty, chronology, or request should be treated as high-impact.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The scan showed a possible lesion.
bad_example: The scan confirmed cancer.
ai_grading_logic: Score both Language and Content/accuracy implications where applicable; do not double-count mechanically, but explain the cross-criterion impact.

title: Repeated systematic errors matter more than isolated slips
canonical_rule: One minor article/preposition slip should not dominate feedback; repeated errors that impede clarity or professional tone should receive greater weight.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: One isolated missing article in an otherwise clear letter.
bad_example: Repeated tense shifts that obscure chronology.
ai_grading_logic: Track frequency, distribution and impact, not merely raw error count.

title: Do not enforce teacher preferences as universal grammar
canonical_rule: A style preference may be suggested, but the AI must not label a standard-English alternative “wrong” unless official OET requirements or grammar justify it.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: However, the pain persisted.
bad_example: Marking sentence-initial However as wrong because a semicolon was not used.
ai_grading_logic: Authority hierarchy: OET official > validated grammar > direct teaching preference for mandatory-error labels.

title: Regional standard-English variation is acceptable
canonical_rule: Accept standard British/Australian/international variants (spelling, punctuation, selected collocations) when consistent and clear.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: organisation / organization; paediatric / pediatric
bad_example: Mixing variants is not automatically a major error.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: OET is international; formal consistency is preferable.

title: Spelling errors are judged by impact and recurrence
canonical_rule: Flag misspellings, especially in clinical terms and names, but distinguish a one-off typo from repeated language-control problems.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: amoxicillin
bad_example: amoxcillin
ai_grading_logic: A misspelled medicine that creates ambiguity is more serious than a harmless typo in a common word.

title: Grammar advice must preserve task content
canonical_rule: When correcting grammar, do not rewrite away clinically relevant facts, alter certainty, or invent information.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Correct syntax while preserving exact dose, date and request.
bad_example: “Improve” the letter by adding a diagnosis not in the notes.
ai_grading_logic: Every language correction must pass a semantic-equivalence check against the case notes.

title: Use complete but natural spoken turns

title: After prepositions use noun/gerund forms
canonical_rule: A preposition is followed by a noun phrase or -ing form, not a bare infinitive.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Purpose: to-infinitive

bad_example: She was referred to cardiology for assess recurrent syncope.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: In order to / so that for explicit purpose
canonical_rule: Use in order to + infinitive or so that + finite clause when a clearer purpose relationship is needed.

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Avoid ambiguous participial clauses
canonical_rule: An -ing clause should logically share its subject with the main clause unless explicitly expressed.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: After discussing the options with Ms Hall, I arranged follow-up.
bad_example: After discussing the options, follow-up was arranged.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: The second is common but leaves the actor implicit; rewrite if ambiguity matters.

title: Preserve diagnostic certainty
canonical_rule: Use may/might/could/suspected/likely/probable/confirmed exactly as supported by the case notes; never upgrade uncertainty.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The findings are suspicious for malignancy.
bad_example: The patient has cancer.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: This is both a grammar/lexis and clinical-accuracy rule.

title: Would for polite requests
canonical_rule: Would/could can soften professional requests without weakening purpose.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: I would be grateful if you could review her urgently.
bad_example: You must review her urgently.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Direct imperatives may be appropriate in emergency protocols but are usually not the tone of a referral letter.

title: Should for recommendation, not certainty
canonical_rule: Use should for recommendation/expectation; do not use it where the notes state a definite plan.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She should continue the exercises as advised.
bad_example: She will continue the exercises as advised.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Use will only if the future action is actually established.

title: Must signals strong necessity
canonical_rule: Use must only when obligation/necessity is supported; otherwise use should/needs to/is advised to.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She must seek urgent care if breathing becomes difficult.
bad_example: She must exercise daily.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: The latter may overstate a routine recommendation.

title: Use real conditionals for safety-netting
canonical_rule: If + present, imperative/modal/future is appropriate for realistic future warning signs.

bad_example: If the swelling will worsen, she should seek urgent review.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Pain location: in/at depend on meaning
canonical_rule: Use pain in + body region for location within an area; at can identify a precise site but is less common in ordinary symptom descriptions.

title: Pain increases with/on/during according to trigger
canonical_rule: Use with for an associated trigger/activity, on + gerund/noun in clinical shorthand-like prose, or during for an event; choose the clearest natural construction.

good_example: The pain increases with movement. / The pain worsens on walking.
bad_example: The pain increases by walking.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Both “with movement” and “on movement/walking” can be correct; do not teach one as universally wrong.

title: Pain relieved by/with
canonical_rule: Use relieved by for the agent/cause of improvement; relieved with is also possible for the means/treatment, but by is usually clearest in clinical prose.

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Comply/adhere to

evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment

bad_example: She has had difficulty adhering with the regimen.

title: Concerned about / concern regarding

title: Allergic to
canonical_rule: Use allergic to + substance.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She is allergic to penicillin.
bad_example: She is allergic from penicillin.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Diagnosed with / diagnosis of
canonical_rule: Use diagnosed with a condition; diagnosis of + condition.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: He was diagnosed with COPD.

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: At risk of / risk for
canonical_rule: At risk of + outcome is standard; risk for also occurs, especially before a condition, but maintain natural professional usage.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She is at increased risk of falls.
bad_example: She is at risk for falling down.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: “Risk for” is common in some healthcare varieties; do not over-penalise a correct regional construction.

title: Associated with / secondary to / due to
canonical_rule: Use causal language that matches certainty.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The cough may be associated with reflux.
bad_example: The cough is due from reflux.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Referred to ... for ...
canonical_rule: Use to for destination/recipient and for for the reason/request.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She was referred to the respiratory team for further assessment.
bad_example: She was referred for the respiratory team to assessment.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Discharged from ... to ...
canonical_rule: Use from for origin and to/into the care of for destination.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: He was discharged from hospital to a rehabilitation facility.
bad_example: He was discharged to hospital from a rehabilitation facility.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Context determines actual direction.

title: However has flexible punctuation
canonical_rule: However may start a sentence followed by a comma, or link independent clauses after a semicolon; it is not restricted to one pattern.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The pain improved. However, swelling persisted. / The pain improved; however, swelling persisted.
bad_example: The pain improved however swelling persisted.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Therefore/consequently have flexible sentence positions
canonical_rule: Conjunctive adverbs can start a new sentence or follow a semicolon when linking independent clauses.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The wound remained infected. Therefore, antibiotics were changed.
bad_example: The wound remained infected, therefore antibiotics were changed.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Although introduces a finite clause
canonical_rule: Use although/even though + subject + verb.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Although the pain improved, she remained unable to work.
bad_example: Although improvement in pain, she remained unable to work.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Despite/in spite of take a noun phrase or gerund
canonical_rule: Use despite/in spite of + noun/-ing; despite the fact that + clause is also possible.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Despite improving, she remained breathless. / Despite the improvement, she remained breathless.
bad_example: Despite she improved, she remained breathless.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Comma after introductory dependent clauses/phrases when helpful
canonical_rule: Use a comma after a substantial introductory clause or phrase to show the boundary.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Despite the improvement, she remains unable to climb stairs.
bad_example: Despite the improvement she remains unable to climb stairs.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Short introductory phrases may sometimes omit a comma, but clarity controls.

title: Because/as/since causal clauses do not obey a single comma rule
canonical_rule: Punctuate causal clauses according to position and meaning; there is no universal rule requiring a comma before as/because.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Treatment was changed because symptoms persisted.
bad_example: Treatment was changed, because symptoms persisted.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: A comma may be justified for a nonessential or contrastive reading, but not by a blanket rule.

title: In addition to/as well as/along with can be punctuated by structure
canonical_rule: These phrases take a noun/gerund complement; commas depend on whether the phrase is integrated or parenthetical.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: In addition to nausea, she reported vomiting. / The rash, along with fever, was noted.
bad_example: In addition to she vomited, she had nausea.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Avoid mechanical linker overload
canonical_rule: Use cohesive devices only where they clarify logic; chronology and paragraphing can provide cohesion without a linker in every sentence.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Her pain worsened overnight. She therefore attended the emergency department.
bad_example: Furthermore... Moreover... In addition... Consequently... in every sentence.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Use and/or/but accurately
canonical_rule: And adds; but contrasts; or presents alternatives. Do not use a connector solely because it sounds formal.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She was afebrile but remained tachycardic.
bad_example: She was afebrile and remained tachycardic.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: The second is grammatical but may misrepresent contrast.

title: Full stops end complete sentences
canonical_rule: Use a full stop to separate complete statements where no stronger relation needs punctuation.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The wound was red. A swab was taken.
bad_example: The wound was red A swab was taken.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Comma after introductory subordinate clause
canonical_rule: A comma usually follows an initial subordinate clause before the main clause.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: When she returned, the swelling had reduced.
bad_example: When she returned the swelling had reduced.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Comma with nonessential appositives
canonical_rule: Use paired commas around nonessential appositive information.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Ms Ali, a 54-year-old teacher, presented with dizziness.
bad_example: Ms Ali, a 54-year-old teacher presented with dizziness.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: No comma between subject and verb
canonical_rule: Do not separate a subject from its verb unless a parenthetical element requires paired commas.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The results of the blood tests were normal.
bad_example: The results of the blood tests, were normal.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Comma before coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
canonical_rule: A comma is commonly used before and/but/so when each side is an independent clause; it may be omitted when clauses are short and closely linked, depending on style.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She remained febrile, so blood cultures were obtained.
bad_example: She remained febrile so, blood cultures were obtained.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Semicolon links closely related independent clauses
canonical_rule: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The pain improved; mobility remained limited.
bad_example: The pain improved; and mobility remained limited.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: A semicolon before a coordinating conjunction is usually unnecessary.

title: Colon introduces an explanation/list after a complete lead-in
canonical_rule: Use a colon after an independent clause that introduces a list, explanation, or elaboration.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She has two current concerns: pain and poor sleep.

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Apostrophe for possession
canonical_rule: Use ’s for most singular nouns/names; for plural nouns ending in s, add an apostrophe. Style guides vary for singular names ending in s, so be consistent.

title: Hyphenate compound modifiers before nouns

canonical_rule: Do not use the compound-modifier form after the verb.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Capitalise sentence starts and proper nouns
canonical_rule: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and proper names, institutions, branded medicines, and eponyms as appropriate.

title: Common disease names are normally lowercase
canonical_rule: Generic disease/condition names are lowercase unless they contain a proper noun or begin a sentence.

title: Use abbreviations only when appropriate to the reader
canonical_rule: Spell out unfamiliar or ambiguous abbreviations; widely understood healthcare abbreviations may be acceptable when the reader’s expertise supports them.

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Avoid note-form dosing abbreviations in a formal letter when clarity may suffer
canonical_rule: Translate ambiguous Latin/frequency abbreviations into plain professional English unless the task/recipient convention clearly supports them.

bad_example: amoxicillin 500 mg tds
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Use numerals with measurements
canonical_rule: Use numerals with doses, measurements, vital signs, ages when paired with units, dates, and exact clinical values.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Use a space between number and most SI units
canonical_rule: In standard scientific style, place a space between a number and unit symbol, except conventional exceptions such as % depending on house style.

good_example: 500 mg; 5 cm

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Keep decimal points and dose units exact
canonical_rule: Do not alter decimal places, units, or magnitude when paraphrasing case notes.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: 0.5 mg
bad_example: 5 mg
ai_grading_logic: Treat a dose/unit change as a high-severity accuracy error, not merely a grammar error.

title: Do not invent reference ranges
canonical_rule: Report clinically relevant values from the case notes; do not add normal ranges or interpretations not supplied unless the task explicitly provides/requests them.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Her potassium was 3.1 mmol/L.
bad_example: Her potassium was 3.1 mmol/L (normal 3.5–5.0) when the range was not in the notes.
ai_grading_logic: Penalise invented clinical data as Content/accuracy, regardless of grammatical correctness.

title: Word-vs-numeral style is secondary to clarity and consistency
canonical_rule: There is no universal OET rule that 1–9 must always be words and 10+ numerals. Use a consistent professional style; numerals are preferred for clinical data.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She has two children and takes 5 mg daily.
bad_example: She has 2 children and takes five mg daily.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Both child-count styles can be acceptable; the dose should remain numerical.

title: Prefer precise clinical-neutral wording
canonical_rule: Choose words that accurately represent the notes without adding judgement or emotional colouring.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: He reported smoking 20 cigarettes daily.
bad_example: He is a terrible heavy smoker.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Patient is not a forbidden word
canonical_rule: “Patient” is acceptable when natural and unambiguous; avoid repetitive or dehumanising use, not the word itself.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: The patient was discharged with community follow-up.
bad_example: Never use the word patient.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: This explicitly overrides the legacy blanket prohibition.

title: Smoker/drinker are not grammatically forbidden but person-first factual wording is often better
canonical_rule: Use factual behaviour descriptions when they are clearer and less judgmental.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She smokes 10 cigarettes per day.
bad_example: She is a smoker.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: “Smoker” is standard English and not automatically an OET error; judge tone/context.

title: Do not replace patient wording with a stronger diagnosis
canonical_rule: Paraphrase only when meaning and certainty remain identical.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She reported feeling tired.
bad_example: She has fatigue.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: “Fatigue” may be a clinical symptom, but it is not always semantically identical to ordinary tiredness.

title: Non-compliance language requires care
canonical_rule: Prefer descriptive, non-judgmental language such as difficulty adhering when supported; “non-compliant” may be accepted if it is the exact case-note concept but can sound judgmental.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: He reported difficulty taking the tablets consistently.
bad_example: He is a non-compliant patient.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably are banned as emotional wording
canonical_rule: Emotive/editorialising adverbs (unfortunately, fortunately, regrettably) and dramatised suffering/suffered must not appear in OET Writing Model Answers; state clinical facts and outcomes factually and objectively. Standard clinical usage of suffering/suffered for a diagnosed event (e.g. "suffered a myocardial infarction") is not emotional wording and remains acceptable.
evidence: Writing Rule Enforcement Addendum Rev5 (10 Sep 2026) owner governance decision, item 1 "G-W-116": the newer clarification supersedes this rule's prior general-English framing per the addendum's own precedence rule.
good_example: The scan could not be completed because of severe claustrophobia.
bad_example: Unfortunately, the poor patient could not tolerate the scan.
ai_grading_logic: Flag any use of unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably, and flag suffering/suffered only when paired with a dramatising intensifier (e.g. "suffered terribly", "the poor patient suffered"). Do not flag suffering/suffered used as the standard factual clinical verb for a diagnosed event.
notes: Superseded the original "do not auto-penalise the word itself" framing on 10 Sep 2026 per explicit owner governance decision; see docs/canonical-rules/README.md change log.

title: Use formal contractions sparingly or not at all in letters

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: A contraction is a genre/style issue, not a catastrophic grammar failure.

ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

canonical_rule: Emotive/editorialising adverbs (unfortunately, fortunately, regrettably) and dramatised suffering/suffered must not appear in OET Writing Model Answers; state clinical facts and outcomes factually and objectively. Standard clinical usage of suffering/suffered for a diagnosed event (e.g. "suffered a myocardial infarction") is not emotional wording and remains acceptable.

ai_grading_logic: Flag any use of unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably, and flag suffering/suffered only when paired with a dramatising intensifier (e.g. "suffered terribly", "the poor patient suffered"). Do not flag suffering/suffered used as the standard factual clinical verb for a diagnosed event.
notes: Superseded the original "do not auto-penalise the word itself" framing on 10 Sep 2026 per explicit owner governance decision; see docs/canonical-rules/README.md change log.

title: Do not invent reference ranges
canonical_rule: Report clinically relevant values from the case notes; do not add normal ranges or interpretations not supplied unless the task explicitly provides/requests them.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: Her potassium was 3.1 mmol/L.
bad_example: Her potassium was 3.1 mmol/L (normal 3.5–5.0) when the range was not in the notes.
ai_grading_logic: Penalise invented clinical data as Content/accuracy, regardless of grammatical correctness.

title: Word-vs-numeral style is secondary to clarity and consistency
canonical_rule: There is no universal OET rule that 1–9 must always be words and 10+ numerals. Use a consistent professional style; numerals are preferred for clinical data.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She has two children and takes 5 mg daily.
bad_example: She has 2 children and takes five mg daily.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: Both child-count styles can be acceptable; the dose should remain numerical.

title: Prefer precise clinical-neutral wording
canonical_rule: Choose words that accurately represent the notes without adding judgement or emotional colouring.

good_example: He reported smoking 20 cigarettes daily.
bad_example: He is a terrible heavy smoker.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Patient is not a forbidden word

bad_example: Never use the word patient.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Smoker/drinker are not grammatically forbidden but person-first factual wording is often better

bad_example: She is a smoker.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Do not replace patient wording with a stronger diagnosis
canonical_rule: Paraphrase only when meaning and certainty remain identical.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: She reported feeling tired.
bad_example: She has fatigue.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: “Fatigue” may be a clinical symptom, but it is not always semantically identical to ordinary tiredness.

title: Non-compliance language requires care
canonical_rule: Prefer descriptive, non-judgmental language such as difficulty adhering when supported; “non-compliant” may be accepted if it is the exact case-note concept but can sound judgmental.
evidence: Standard English grammar; OET Language / Resources of Grammar & Expression alignment
good_example: He reported difficulty taking the tablets consistently.
bad_example: He is a non-compliant patient.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

title: Unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably are banned as emotional wording
canonical_rule: Emotive/editorialising adverbs (unfortunately, fortunately, regrettably) and dramatised suffering/suffered must not appear in OET Writing Model Answers; state clinical facts and outcomes factually and objectively. Standard clinical usage of suffering/suffered for a diagnosed event (e.g. "suffered a myocardial infarction") is not emotional wording and remains acceptable.
evidence: Writing Rule Enforcement Addendum Rev5 (10 Sep 2026) owner governance decision, item 1 "G-W-116": the newer clarification supersedes this rule's prior general-English framing per the addendum's own precedence rule.
good_example: The scan could not be completed because of severe claustrophobia.
bad_example: Unfortunately, the poor patient could not tolerate the scan.
ai_grading_logic: Flag any use of unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably, and flag suffering/suffered only when paired with a dramatising intensifier (e.g. "suffered terribly", "the poor patient suffered"). Do not flag suffering/suffered used as the standard factual clinical verb for a diagnosed event.
notes: Superseded the original "do not auto-penalise the word itself" framing on 10 Sep 2026 per explicit owner governance decision; see docs/canonical-rules/README.md change log.

title: Use formal contractions sparingly or not at all in letters

good_example: She did not attend.
bad_example: She didn’t attend.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.
notes: A contraction is a genre/style issue, not a catastrophic grammar failure.

bad_example: On 03/02/2026, on 05/02/2026, on 07/02/2026... for every minor event.
ai_grading_logic: Flag only when the form is ungrammatical, changes meaning, reduces clarity, or is repeatedly inappropriate for formal healthcare communication.

canonical_rule: Emotive/editorialising adverbs (unfortunately, fortunately, regrettably) and dramatised suffering/suffered must not appear in OET Writing Model Answers; state clinical facts and outcomes factually and objectively. Standard clinical usage of suffering/suffered for a diagnosed event (e.g. "suffered a myocardial infarction") is not emotional wording and remains acceptable.

ai_grading_logic: Flag any use of unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably, and flag suffering/suffered only when paired with a dramatising intensifier (e.g. "suffered terribly", "the poor patient suffered"). Do not flag suffering/suffered used as the standard factual clinical verb for a diagnosed event.
notes: Superseded the original "do not auto-penalise the word itself" framing on 10 Sep 2026 per explicit owner governance decision; see docs/canonical-rules/README.md change log.

title: Separate language from clinical knowledge
